subject: Questions about working with clustered populations and high density estimates from NegBin mixtures

messages.author: 45906a28df896f54
messages.subject: Questions about working with clustered populations and high density estimates from NegBin mixtures
parts:
Hi Everyone,
I'm posting this as a follow-up to a previous post (which I have deleted as I was able to answer my question on my own before anyone was able to respond) and have since come up with more specific and detailed questions to resulting issues.

Some quick background info:

We had 3 observers conduct 3 rounds of 10-min long point-count surveys at 150 points (i.e. each observer visited each point once) over 10 weeks. The species we are working with has a high tendency to flock together, so rather than record distances for individual birds we recorded distances to the center of each cluster per recommendations from Buckland et al (cluster size ranged from 1-14 individuals with a mean of~3).

My first question is in regards to how I should handle the fact that I'm working with clusters and which function I should use to do so as I expect that cluster size is likely to be one of the most important covariates affecting detection. My first thought was model detection of clusters and then use cluster size as a covariate, rather than model detection of individuals. For example my observation data from point 1 would look something like:

Point            Observation           Distance            Cluster_Size
1                  1                            46                       1
1                  1                            87                       4

Rather than:

Point            Observation           Distance
1                  1                             46
1                  4                             87

I would then try to estimate the total abundance of clusters across my study region and extrapolate that out to abundance of individuals using either mean cluster size or a size-biased regression analysis similar to what is possible with Program Distance. However, my understanding is that doing it this way would require coding cluster size as an observation level covariate. From what I've been able to glean from the help files and vignettes I can only include observation level covariates if I use colext(), gmultmix(), or gpcount() and the associated unmarkedFrames. However, because I had repeated visits to each site and have distance data I feel like I should be using gdistsamp() for all of my analyses, which I don't think can incorporate observation level covariates (though please correct me if I'm wrong!!!!).

Question 1:

Is taking this approach and modeling detection of clusters rather than individuals appropriate, and if so what function should I use/how should I structure my data to do so given that I would like to model cluster size as a covariate and used a repeated visits design? Can any function in unmarked handle both repeated visits and observation level covariates for distance data?


My second question has to do with some funky results I keep getting in my preliminary analyses, I should note that this pattern keeps occurring regardless of whether I try to model detection of clusters (which I have done but have not been able to incorporate cluster size as a covariate into the model yet) or model detection of individuals. In general models using a negative binomial mixture consistently out-perform those using poisson. In many ways I expected this outcome, especially since my data has a LOT of 0 observations, which is partly why repeated visits were necessary. Top ranking models using the NB also do well on bootstrapped GoF tests (specifically Freeman-Tukey). However, the density/abundance estimates I get from using NB mixtures are all unreasonably high (i.e. ~10X the upper limit of what I would expect). In previous discussions I have seen some people mention that this can occur when using NB, and even found a comment from one contributor referencing a paper by Johnson circa 2009 from Conservation Biology that discusses this issue, but have been unable to find said paper and am unclear on why this happens with NB or what to do about it.

Question 2:
Why are my abundance estimates with negative binomial ~10X larger than the ones I'm getting from poisson, and does anyone have any advice for what I should do to address this problem? My impression from working with these birds is that despite the large number of 0 observations detectability is fairly high but availability extremely low, would accounting for availability resolve this problem or should I ignore NegBin entirely despite the fact that for some reasons it seems appropriate?

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated, and thanks for any help.

Best,
Nathaniel

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Questions about working with clustered populations and high density estimates from NegBin mixtures
parts: However, because I had repeated visits to each site and have distance data I feel like I should be using gdistsamp() for all of my analyses, which I don't think can incorporate observation level covariates (though please correct me if I'm wrong!!!!).
I believe that in gdistsamp, yearlySiteCovs (one input for the frame) can act as obsCovs...ie., yearly site covs can vary by visit.

Question 2:
Why are my abundance estimates with negative binomial ~10X larger than the ones I'm getting from poisson, and does anyone have any advice for what I should do to address this problem? My impression from working with these birds is that despite the large number of 0 observations detectability is fairly high but availability extremely low, would accounting for availability resolve this problem or should I ignore NegBin entirely despite the fact that for some reasons it seems appropriate?

If you have AHM vol 1., there's a good section describing trade-offs between Neg-Bin and Poisson (I think in the N-mixture chapter). Negative Binomial mixtures often fit the data better, but can also result in strange estimates.  A strongly Zero-inflated Poission distribution has extra Poisson variability -> Poor Poisson fit -> NegBinomial selection, even though NegBin may not be a realistic assumed distribution--the paper I think you are looking for is by Joseph et al. 2009 (Ecological Applications).  NBin might well describe the flock-size fairly well, but your description suggests that it may not describe the 'abundance' of flocks all that well.

I don't know that incorporating availability will 'fix' issues of abundance estimation, but it does provide a little more flexibility for thinking about how abundance might be interpreted. 

Is taking this approach and modeling detection of clusters rather than individuals appropriate...?

Punting on this. A more complex approach that comes to mind might involve working with spatial distance model (maybe the underlying point process describing individual locations is over-dispersed), but this seems like a tricky problem (Abundance influences detection influences estimation of abundance). Treating flock size as influencing detection makes sense (don't know whether a covariate, or an off-set, or some other functional relationship is best). I'd just suggest that for trying to get at overall bird population size by multiplying the estimated number of flocks by average cluster size or whatever, that the observed flocks seem likely to be bigger than the flocks missed. 


John

parts:
Hi John,
Thanks for all of your suggestions, they were really helpful and I appreciate your help. You've given me some good things to think about regarding clusters and NB. I have a copy of AHM vol 1. and will be sure to check the chapter in question as well as the Joseph paper. However, I have a quick follow up I could still use some advice on as I'm afraid I may not have been as clear as I could though in describing what I'm calling "observation-level" covariates and feel I should elaborate...

The way I see it I have three "levels" of covariates that could be affecting detection/abundance, which for the current purposes I'll call site-level, survey-level, and observation-level. Site-level covariates are pretty obvious (i.e. habitat metrics) as they don't change between visits and gdistsamp can clearly handle these as what unmarked calls "sitecovs". What I'll call survey-level covariates are things like observer, wind speed, etc that vary between visits. As you described, gdistsamp can handle these as yearlySitecovs and I've actually already incorporated these into some of my early models to investigate differences between observers. What I'm calling observation level covariates (in this case just cluster size) are things that vary within a single visit and affect each individual detection. I feel this is important because we often detected more than one cluster during an individual visit to a site, so I can't apply just 1 value for cluster size to a single visit.

Is there a way I can incorporate this 3rd level of covariate that varies from detection to detection and is specific to each individual observation into gdistsamp?


Thanks again for all the help!

Nathaniel
